artifacts.body:
S: 45-year-old male, 9 days post-return from 3-week trip to Kumasi, Ghana, presents with 4 days of high fever (Tmax 39.4°C), drenching sweats, headache, myalgias, one episode of vomiting, mild diarrhea, and new dark urine today. No malaria chemoprophylaxis taken. Took leftover amoxicillin x2 days without improvement. No rash, no bleeding. Son (age 12) traveled with patient and remains well.

O: Vitals as above (febrile, tachycardic, borderline hypotensive). Mild scleral icterus. Patient-reported LUQ fullness/tenderness on self-palpation (not clinician-verified, requires in-person confirmation). Urine visually dark on camera. No rash or petechiae. No neck stiffness.

A: High pretest probability malaria, potentially severe given jaundice and possible splenomegaly/hemolysis (splenomegaly unconfirmed pending formal exam). Treat as medical emergency.

P: STAT ED referral for thick/thin smear, RDT, CBC, combined BMP/hepatic panel (bilirubin/LFTs, renal function, glucose). Counsel patient on urgency, arrange transport, do not delay for outpatient labs.

facts.chart: Patient reports 4 days of fever up to 39.4°C with sweats, headache, and muscle aches after returning from Ghana 9 days ago.

facts.says: I was in Kumasi for three weeks visiting my family. Got back nine days ago.

facts.chart: Fevers occurring daily, Tmax 39.4°C, with associated drenching sweats and chills.
facts.says: The fever comes and goes but it keeps spiking really high, and then I just soak through my shirt with sweat.

facts.says: I didn't take any malaria pills. I grew up there, so I figured I'd still have some immunity from when I was a kid.

facts.says: I had some old amoxicillin from a dental thing a while back, so I took that for two days hoping it would help, but it didn't do much.

facts.says: My stomach's been a little loose the last couple days, nothing crazy, no blood or anything.

facts.says: No, I haven't noticed any rash anywhere.

facts.says: The headache is pretty bad, mostly in the front of my head, but my vision's fine.

facts.chart: Denies neck stiffness or photophobia.
facts.says: No stiff neck, and light doesn't really bother my eyes any more than usual.

facts.chart: Denies cough, shortness of breath, or chest pain.
facts.says: No cough, no trouble breathing, nothing like that.

facts.chart: Denies dysuria or urinary frequency changes aside from color.
facts.says: It doesn't burn or anything when I go, it's just the color that changed.

facts.chart: Decreased appetite over past 4 days; tolerating fluids reasonably well.
facts.says: I haven't really felt like eating much, but I've been able to keep drinking water okay.

facts.chart: 12-year-old son traveled with patient to Ghana and remains asymptomatic.
facts.says: My son came with me, he's twelve, and he's totally fine, no symptoms at all.

facts.chart: Reports frequent evening outdoor activity in Kumasi with inconsistent bed net use and no insect repellent use.
facts.says: I was outside a lot in the evenings visiting people, and I didn't really use a mosquito net every night or any bug spray.

facts.says: I ate some street food here and there, and probably drank tap water a couple times without thinking about it.

facts.says: No animal bites, no ticks that I noticed, and I didn't go swimming in any rivers or lakes.

facts.says: I had malaria a bunch of times as a kid back home, but that was over twenty years ago. Nothing since I moved to the US.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient believes childhood malaria exposure in Ghana gives him lasting immunity, so he skipped prophylaxis.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Primary care note from 14 months ago documents that malaria prophylaxis and travel counseling were offered and discussed, but the patient did not return for a dedicated travel consultation before departure, and no prophylaxis was prescribed or taken.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Childhood exposure to malaria does not confer durable immunity in adulthood, especially after years away from an endemic area; this is a common and dangerous misconception that clinicians must proactively address, as missed opportunity for travel counseling contributed to this presentation.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient reports taking leftover amoxicillin for 2 days hoping it would treat his fever.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Medication list confirms amoxicillin was self-directed, not clinician-ordered, and is not an appropriate or effective empiric therapy for malaria, which likely explains why his symptoms did not improve and in fact worsened with new jaundice and dark urine.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Self-treatment with leftover or mismatched antibiotics can delay appropriate diagnosis and treatment of malaria and may mask or complicate the clinical picture; empiric antibacterial therapy has no role in suspected malaria.

objectives.text: Elicit a complete travel, exposure, and chemoprophylaxis history to establish malaria as the leading diagnosis in a febrile returning traveler.
Recognize and correct the common misconception that childhood exposure to malaria confers lasting immunity in adulthood.
Identify clinical features suggestive of potentially severe or complicated malaria (jaundice, dark urine suggesting hemolysis, splenomegaly, tachycardia) that mandate emergency-level urgency.

Correctly order the appropriate same-day diagnostic workup for suspected malaria (thick/thin smear, rapid antigen test, CBC, combined metabolic/hepatic panel for renal function, bilirubin/LFTs, and glucose) and recognize this cannot be deferred to routine outpatient labs.
Recognize that leftover or inappropriate self-treatment with antibiotics does not address malaria and may contribute to diagnostic delay, and counsel accordingly.
Communicate the urgency of same-day emergency department referral effectively to a patient who is reluctant due to work and cost concerns, while respecting his autonomy and circumstances.

answerKey.primaryProblem: Suspected malaria (clinical features raising concern for possible severe/complicated disease, pending confirmatory testing) in a febrile returning traveler from a malaria-endemic region, without chemoprophylaxis
differential: Plasmodium falciparum or other species malaria (leading diagnosis)
keyFindings: 9 days post-return from 3-week stay in malaria-endemic Kumasi, Ghana
No malaria chemoprophylaxis taken due to false belief in childhood-acquired immunity
4 days of high fever (Tmax 39.4°C) with drenching sweats, headache, myalgias
New dark/tea-colored urine today, raising concern for possible hemolysis (unconfirmed, labs pending)
Mild scleral icterus on camera exam
Patient-reported left upper quadrant fullness/tenderness on self-palpation (not a clinician-verified exam finding), raising concern for possible splenomegaly that requires in-person confirmation
Tachycardia (HR 112) and borderline hypotension on vitals
No rash, no bleeding, no neck stiffness, no confusion — helps narrow differential and assess for severity
No parasitemia, hemolysis, or organ function labs available yet; findings are suggestive but not yet diagnostic of severe malaria
plan: Counsel patient that this is a medical emergency requiring same-day in-person evaluation, not manageable via telehealth alone
Arrange immediate referral to emergency department for STAT thick and thin blood smears for malaria parasites and species identification
Order STAT rapid malaria antigen test as an adjunct, understanding smear remains gold standard
Order STAT CBC with differential to assess for anemia, thrombocytopenia, parasitemia clues

Order STAT combined basic metabolic panel and hepatic function panel (renal function, glucose, total/direct bilirubin, AST/ALT) given scleral icterus, dark urine, and need to assess for hypoglycemia (no home glucometer available)
Advise discontinuing further self-directed antibiotic use; amoxicillin has no role in treating malaria

Address patient's cost and work concerns empathetically while reinforcing non-negotiable urgency of same-day evaluation, explaining that current findings are concerning but require labs and formal exam to confirm severity

Coordinate with emergency department / inpatient team for admission and initiation of appropriate antimalarial therapy once species and severity are confirmed, as this is beyond the scope of this telehealth visit to prescribe before results
Provide travel health education for future trips, including need for chemoprophylaxis regardless of childhood history or perceived immunity
Document mismatch between patient's belief in lasting immunity and documented missed travel counseling opportunity for future quality improvement
redFlags: Fever in a returning traveler from a malaria-endemic area is a medical emergency until proven otherwise
Jaundice/scleral icterus combined with dark urine raises concern for hemolysis, though this requires lab confirmation
Patient-reported LUQ fullness (unverified by formal exam), tachycardia, and borderline hypotension warrant urgent in-person assessment and formal exam, not deferred outpatient testing
Risk of rapid clinical deterioration, including cerebral malaria, severe anemia, acute kidney injury, or hypoglycemia, can occur within hours in falciparum malaria if confirmed
Delay in diagnosis and treatment due to patient reluctance (work, cost) must be addressed directly given life-threatening potential
educationPoints: Childhood immunity to malaria wanes significantly after years of non-exposure living outside endemic areas and should never be relied upon to skip prophylaxis
All travelers to malaria-endemic regions, including those originally from or visiting family in such regions (VFR travelers), are at risk and should receive pre-travel counseling and chemoprophylaxis
Fever in a returning traveler always warrants a travel and exposure history as part of the initial assessment, and malaria must be excluded urgently given its potential lethality
Thick and thin blood smears remain the diagnostic gold standard for malaria and must be obtained urgently, often requiring repeat smears if initial testing is negative but suspicion remains high
Self-treatment with leftover antibiotics is a common but potentially harmful practice that can mask symptoms or delay appropriate care without providing any benefit against malaria
Clear, empathetic communication about the seriousness of a diagnosis can help patients overcome barriers related to work and financial concerns and accept urgent care recommendations

Remote self-reported findings (e.g., self-palpation tenderness) are suggestive but not equivalent to a formal clinical exam, and should be framed as findings to be confirmed in person rather than definitive diagnoses

patient.name: Kwame Asante
patient.appearance: A well-built man with short greying hair, appearing fatigued and flushed, wearing a plain grey t-shirt. He is seated on a couch in a dimly lit living room, occasionally wiping his forehead, with a blanket nearby and a glass of water visible on a side table.

persona.personality: Articulate, practical, and somewhat stoic; tends to downplay symptoms initially but answers directly once asked.
persona.communicationStyle: Speaks in clear, organized sentences, asks clarifying questions, appreciates straightforward explanations without excessive jargon.
persona.emotionalState: Mildly anxious but trying to stay composed; frustrated at the inconvenience of being sick and worried about missing work obligations.
persona.background: Kwame immigrated to the United States from Ghana in his twenties for graduate school and has taught high school mathematics in Columbus for the past 15 years. He is married with two children, including the 12-year-old son who traveled with him. He visits family in Kumasi roughly every two to three years and takes pride in staying connected to his roots.
speechExamples: I know my body pretty well, and this doesn't feel like a regular flu.
I really can't afford to miss a day of school tomorrow, I have a big exam to proctor.
Growing up, I had malaria so many times I just figured I'd built up some resistance to it.
Is this something a round of antibiotics can clear up quickly?
I appreciate you being straightforward with me about how serious this might be.
concerns: Wants to know if he can still go to work tomorrow
Worried about the cost of an emergency department visit
Confused about why he might have malaria despite childhood exposure
Concerned about what the dark urine means

scenario.studentBrief: You are the infectious disease fellow conducting a telehealth consultation. Kwame Asante, a 45-year-old man, is calling 9 days after returning from a 3-week trip to Kumasi, Ghana, with several days of fever. Review his history and current status, and determine next steps.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Fever and body aches for 4 days after returning from travel to Ghana
scenario.openingLine: I've had this fever for about four days now, really high, with drenching sweats, and my head and whole body ache. I just got back from Ghana about a week and a half ago.
tasks: Obtain a focused travel, exposure, and fever history
Assess for clinical findings via remote exam techniques (skin, sclerae, abdomen, urine inspection)
Determine appropriate same-day diagnostic workup and explain the urgency
Address the patient's questions and concerns about work and cost
Formulate and clearly communicate an urgent disposition plan

profile.setting: Telehealth video visit, patient at home in Columbus, Ohio, seated in his living room
profile.summary: A 45-year-old Ghanaian-American teacher presents via telehealth with 4 days of high fever, sweats, and new dark urine 9 days after returning from unprotected travel to Kumasi, Ghana, without malaria chemoprophylaxis. The case teaches recognition of malaria as a medical emergency in a returning traveler, remote assessment for signs of severity (jaundice, splenomegaly, hemolysis), and urgent same-day escalation to emergency care despite patient reluctance tied to work and cost concerns.
profile.title: Travel-Related Fever in a Returning Traveler from Ghana: Malaria Until Proven Otherwise
